presentation_slides.title: What is Physics?
content: Physics is a branch of natural science.
It aims to describe the fundamental aspects of our universe.
The word 'physics' comes from the Greek word 'phusis', meaning nature.
Physics attempts to describe the basic mechanisms that make our universe behave the way it does.

presentation_slides.title: What Physics Explains
content: Working principles of cars, airplanes, and space-rockets.
Working principles of refrigerators, radios, and televisions.
Daily utensils and tools.
Physical phenomena like walking on a smooth plane and why an electric fan rotates.

presentation_slides.title: Importance of Physics
content: Helps discover unknown parts of nature.
Makes you familiar with the modern world.
Helps you understand concepts in other subjects like Biology, Chemistry, Geology, and Astronomy.
Provides various career opportunities.

presentation_slides.title: Career Opportunities in Physics
content: Transportation
Aviation and space science
Medicine
Forensic and military science
Meteorology and metrology

presentation_slides.title: Who is a Physicist?
content: A person who studies physics is called a physicist.
Physicists study concepts, relationships, principles, and laws of nature.

presentation_slides.title: Branches of Physics
content: Physics has expanded into many branches.
Branches include: Mechanics, Acoustics, Optics, Thermodynamics, Electromagnetism, Nuclear Physics, Astrophysics, etc.

presentation_slides.title: Mechanics
content: Deals with the motion of an object with or without the reference of force.
Divided into Quantum Mechanics (behavior of smallest particles) and Classical Mechanics (laws of motion of forces and physical objects).

presentation_slides.title: Other Branches of Physics
content: Acoustics: Study of sound and its transmission, production, and effects.
Optics: Study of the behavior, propagation, and properties of light.
Thermodynamics: Study of thermal energy and the transfer of heat.
Electromagnetism: Study of electromagnetic force like electric fields, light, magnetic fields.
Nuclear Physics: Study of the structure, properties, and reactions of atomic nuclei.
Astrophysics: Application of physics principles to study astronomical objects and phenomena.

presentation_slides.title: Physics and Other Sciences
content: Physics is the foundation of many important scientific disciplines.
Chemistry: Rooted in atomic and molecular physics.
Engineering: Applies physics for structural stability, acoustics, heating, lighting, and cooling.
Geology: Uses physics in radioactive dating, earthquake analysis, and heat transfer.
Biophysics: Applies physics principles to study biological phenomena.
Geophysics: Applies physics principles to study the Earth.
Medical Physics: Uses physics for diagnostics and therapy like X-rays and MRI.

presentation_slides.title: Classical vs Modern Physics
content: Classical Physics: Physics as it developed from the Renaissance to the end of the 19th century.
Modern Physics: Based on revolutionary discoveries starting at the beginning of the 20th century.
Many laws of classical physics were modified, leading to dramatic changes in technology, society, and our view of the universe.

presentation_slides.title: Isaac Newton
content: Laid foundations for classical physics/classical mechanics.
Formulated three laws of motion (Newton's laws of motion).
Showed how the principle of universal gravitation explains the behavior of falling bodies on Earth and planets/celestial bodies.

presentation_slides.title: Michael Faraday
content: Contributed to the field of electromagnetism.
In 1821, produced mechanical motion using a permanent magnet and electric current.
Invented the world's first electric generator by converting magnetic force into electrical force.

presentation_slides.title: James Prescott Joule
content: Studied the nature of heat and discovered its relationship to mechanical work.
His work led to the law of conservation of energy.
Helped lay the foundation for the first law of thermodynamics.

presentation_slides.title: Marie Curie
content: Conducted pioneering research in nuclear physics, particularly on radioactivity.
Considered the mother of modern nuclear physics.
Discovered the elements polonium and radium.

presentation_slides.title: Albert Einstein
content: Known for developing the theory of relativity.
His theory had a profound impact on classical mechanics and the philosophy of physics.
Made important contributions to the development of quantum mechanics.
Widely acknowledged as one of the greatest physicists of all time.

presentation_slides.title: Measurement Scales
content: A scale on a measuring device contains markings that show a certain amount of what is being measured.
The number of marks depends on how accurate a measurement can be.
As the number of marks increases, the precision of the device also increases.

presentation_slides.title: Standards in Measurement
content: A standard must be readily accessible and possess a property that can be measured reliably.
Measurements taken by different people in different places must yield the same result.
Lack of standard measurement leads to inaccuracy and bias.
The SI system (International System of Units) is an adaptation of the metric system.

presentation_slides.title: SI Units of Fundamental Quantities
content: The seven basic quantities are: length (m), mass (kg), time (s), temperature (K), current (A), amount of substance (mol), and luminous intensity (cd).
Length: Meter (m) is the SI unit, defined as the distance traveled by light in vacuum in 1/299792458 seconds.
Time: Second (s) is the SI unit, defined as 9,192,631,770 times the period of vibration of radiation from the cesium-133 atom.
Mass: Kilogram (kg) is the SI unit, defined using the Planck constant (h).

presentation_slides.title: Scientific Notation
content: Scientific notation is a way of writing very large or very small numbers.
General form: d × 10^n, where d is a decimal number between 0 and 10, and n is an integer.
If n > 0, the decimal point moves to the right.
If n < 0, the decimal point moves to the left.

presentation_slides.title: Significant Figures and Prefixes
content: Significant Figures: Each non-zero digit is significant. Zeroes are counted if they are between two non-zero digits or at the end of a decimal part.
When adding/subtracting, the answer should have the same number of decimal places as the term with the fewest decimal places.
When multiplying/dividing, the answer should have the same number of significant figures as the quantity with the fewest.
Prefixes: Used to modify units for very large or small sizes. Examples: kilo (10^3), milli (10^-3), micro (10^-6).

presentation_slides.title: Measurement
content: Measurement is the process of comparing an unknown quantity with another quantity of its kind (called the unit of measurement).
It involves three key elements: the physical quantity to be measured, the necessary measuring tools, and the units of measurements used.

presentation_slides.title: Measuring Length
content: Length is a fundamental physical quantity describing the distance between two points.
The SI unit of length is the meter (m).
Non-SI units include: millimeter (mm), centimeter (cm), and kilometer (km).
Instruments: meter stick, tape measure.

presentation_slides.title: Measuring Mass and Time
content: Mass: The amount of matter contained in a body. The SI unit is the kilogram (kg). Instruments: beam balance.
Time: Describes the duration between the beginning and end of an event. The SI unit is the second (s). Instruments: clocks, watches.

presentation_slides.title: Laboratory Safety Rules
content: Always wear lab safety goggles.
Avoid wearing baggy clothing, bulky jewelry, and open-toed shoes.
NEVER work alone in the laboratory.
Do not eat, drink, apply cosmetics, or chew gum in the laboratory.
Report all accidents to the teacher immediately.
Exercise caution when working with electrical equipment.
Wash hands thoroughly after participating in any laboratory activity.

presentation_slides.title: Physical Quantities
content: A physical quantity is anything that you can measure.
Measured values are described in terms of number and unit.
Classified as Fundamental (or Basic) and Derived physical quantities.

presentation_slides.title: Fundamental Physical Quantities
content: Can be measured directly.
Cannot be described in terms of other physical quantities.
The units used are called fundamental units.
There are seven fundamental quantities: length (m), mass (kg), time (s), temperature (K), current (A), amount of substance (mol), and luminous intensity (cd).

presentation_slides.title: Derived Physical Quantities
content: Depend on one or more fundamental quantities for their measurements.
Units are called derived units.
Examples: Area (m²), Volume (m³), Speed (m/s), Density (kg/m³), Force (N = kg·m/s²), Work (J = kg·m²/s²), Pressure (Pa = kg/(m·s²)).

presentation_slides.title: Scalar and Vector Quantities
content: Scalar Quantity: Has only magnitude (size). Examples: distance, mass, time, temperature, energy.
Vector Quantity: Has both magnitude and direction. Examples: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force.
A vector can be represented by a bold letter or a letter with an arrow (e.g., S or S with an arrow).

presentation_slides.title: Unit Conversion
content: Conversion between different units of measurement for the same physical quantity.
Typically through multiplicative conversion factors.
Length: 1 km = 1000 m, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 m = 1000 mm.
Mass: 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 tonne = 1000 kg.
Time: 1 hr = 60 min, 1 min = 60 s, 1 day = 24 hours.

presentation_slides.title: Position and Motion
content: Motion: A continuous change in position of an object relative to a fixed object called a reference frame.
Frame of Reference: A set of coordinates used to determine positions of objects.
Position: A measurement of a location, with respect to some reference point (usually an origin).
An object is at rest if its position does not change with time in a reference frame. It is in motion if its position changes.

presentation_slides.title: Distance vs Displacement
content: Distance: The total path length traveled by a body. It is a scalar quantity.
Displacement: The change in position of a body in a certain direction. It is a vector quantity.
The SI unit for both is the meter (m).
Displacement is independent of the path length taken.
Displacement = X_f - X_i (final position - initial position).

presentation_slides.title: Comparing Distance and Displacement
content: Distance depends on the path followed.
Displacement depends only on the initial and final positions.
Distance can be more than or equal to the magnitude of displacement.
The magnitude of displacement can be less than or equal to the distance.

presentation_slides.title: Speed
content: Speed is the rate at which an object changes its location.
It is a scalar quantity (has magnitude but no direction).
SI unit: meter per second (m/s).
Formula: Speed = Distance / Time.

presentation_slides.title: Average Speed
content: Average speed is the total distance traveled divided by the total time taken.
Formula: Average Speed = Total Distance / Total Time.
It is a scalar quantity.

presentation_slides.title: Instantaneous Speed
content: Instantaneous speed is the speed at a specific instant in time.
It is shown by a speedometer.
Mathematically: v_ins = Δs / Δt as Δt approaches 0.
It is a scalar quantity.

presentation_slides.title: Velocity
content: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement.
It is a vector quantity (has both magnitude and direction).
SI unit: meter per second (m/s).
Average Velocity: Total displacement divided by total time.
Average velocity points in the same direction as the displacement.

presentation_slides.title: Instantaneous Velocity
content: Instantaneous velocity is the velocity at a specific instant in time.
For uniform motion, average and instantaneous velocities are the same.
The magnitude of instantaneous velocity is called instantaneous speed.

presentation_slides.title: Acceleration
content: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
It is a vector quantity.
SI unit: meter per second squared (m/s²).
Acceleration occurs when velocity changes in magnitude (speed), direction, or both.
Formula: Average Acceleration = (v_f - v_i) / (t_f - t_i).

presentation_slides.title: Deceleration
content: Deceleration is negative acceleration.
Occurs when the velocity of a body decreases.
If a body starts from rest, initial velocity is zero (v_i = 0).
If a body comes to rest, final velocity is zero (v_f = 0).

presentation_slides.title: Uniform Motion
content: Motion along a straight line with a constant velocity (constant speed and direction).
The object travels equal distances in equal time intervals.
Acceleration is zero (a = 0).
Average velocity and instantaneous velocity are the same at all times.
Examples: A car moving on a straight road with a fixed speed, an airplane flying with constant speed in a given direction.

presentation_slides.title: Position-Time (s-t) Graphs
content: Indicates the position of an object at any time.
The slope of an s-t graph represents the velocity of the object.
A constant slope means uniform velocity.
Slope = (change in position) / (change in time) = Δx / Δt = v.

presentation_slides.title: Velocity-Time (v-t) Graphs
content: Shows how the velocity of an object changes with time.
The slope of a v-t graph represents the acceleration of the object.
The area under a v-t graph represents the distance covered by the object.
In uniform motion, the v-t graph is a horizontal line (constant velocity).

presentation_slides.title: Speed Limit and Traffic Safety
content: Speed limits are set to ensure traffic safety.
Vehicles moving at very high speed can cause accidents.
A speedometer is a device used to measure the instantaneous speed of a car.
It is important to keep speeds at an optimum level to save lives and avoid property damage.

presentation_slides.title: What is Force?
content: A force is a push or a pull exerted on a body.
It changes the state of motion of the body (velocity) or causes deformation (change in shape or size).
Force is a vector quantity (magnitude and direction).
SI unit: Newton (N).
Examples: Friction force, normal force, and the force of gravity.

presentation_slides.title: Contact vs Non-Contact Forces
content: Contact Forces: Involve physical contact between objects.
Examples: Applied forces, normal forces, frictional forces, spring forces.
Non-Contact Forces: Do not involve physical contact.
Examples: Magnetic force, gravitational force.

presentation_slides.title: Measuring Force and Weight
content: Force is measured using the deformation of a spring.
Weight is the magnitude of the gravitational force acting on a body.
Weight is measured in Newtons.
Weight is directed towards the center of the Earth.

presentation_slides.title: Newton's First Law (Law of Inertia)
content: A body continues to be in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless it is acted on by an unbalanced force.
Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist any attempt to change its velocity.
Mass is a measure of inertia.
An inertial frame is one in which Newton's first law is valid.

presentation_slides.title: Newton's Second Law
content: The acceleration of a body is directly proportional to the net force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass.
Formula: F = ma (Force = mass × acceleration).
1 N is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s².
Weight (W) = mg, where g = 9.8 m/s² (acceleration due to gravity).

presentation_slides.title: Newton's Third Law
content: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
Forces always act in pairs.
If object 1 exerts a force on object 2 (F_12), then object 2 exerts an equal and opposite force on object 1 (F_21 = -F_12).
Action and reaction forces act on different objects.

presentation_slides.title: Friction Force
content: Friction is the resistance to motion of an object from a surface it is in contact with.
It is very important in everyday life (walking, vehicle motion).
It is denoted by 'f'.
Classified into two main types: Static friction and Kinetic friction.

presentation_slides.title: Static and Kinetic Friction
content: Static Friction: Exists between two surfaces in contact when one body tends to slide over the other without moving.
It requires a large force to overcome.
Kinetic Friction: Exists between two contacting surfaces when one slides or rolls over the other.
Its effect on motion is less than that of static friction.
Friction depends on the normal force and the nature of the surfaces (roughness).

presentation_slides.title: Scientific Meaning of Work
content: In physics, work is done when a force causes an object to move.
The force must be applied in the same direction as the direction of displacement.
Formula: W = F_parallel × S (Work = Force parallel to displacement × Displacement).
Work is a scalar quantity.
SI unit: Joule (J). 1 J = 1 N·m.

presentation_slides.title: Conditions for Work
content: Work is only done when the force and displacement are in the same direction.
No work is done if the force is perpendicular to the displacement.
Example: Holding an object stationary requires effort but does no work because there is no displacement.

presentation_slides.title: Energy and Kinetic Energy
content: Energy is the capacity to do work.
It is a scalar quantity.
SI unit: Joule (J).
Kinetic Energy (E_k): Energy possessed by an object due to its motion.
Formula: E_k = 1/2 × m × v².
Depends on the mass and speed of the object.

presentation_slides.title: Potential Energy
content: Potential Energy: Stored energy in an object by virtue of its position or configuration.
Gravitational Potential Energy (E_p): Energy of an object held in a vertical position.
Formula: E_p = m × g × h (mass × acceleration due to gravity × height).
Depends on the height and mass of the object.
Mechanical Energy = Kinetic Energy + Potential Energy.

presentation_slides.title: Power
content: Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred.
It is a scalar quantity.
Formula: P = W / t or P = E / t.
SI unit: Watt (W). 1 W = 1 J/s.
A higher power means work is done more quickly.

presentation_slides.title: What are Simple Machines?
content: A simple machine is a device that requires a single force to do mechanical work.
They do not create energy, but transfer mechanical energy.
They make work easier by:
- Changing the direction of force.
- Multiplying speed or distance.
- Multiplying force.
Effort: The force applied to a machine.
Load: The force exerted by the machine.

presentation_slides.title: Simple Machines at Home
content: Simple machines are used extensively in homes.
They magnify or change the direction of force.
Examples: Scissors, knives, bottle openers, ramps, staplers.
They make tasks like cutting, lifting, and binding easier.

presentation_slides.title: Simple Machines at Work
content: Simple machines are the building blocks of more complex machines.
Used in various workplaces.
Examples: Levers, pulleys, wheels and axles, inclined planes in tools and equipment.

presentation_slides.title: Six Types of Simple Machines
content: 1. Lever
2. Wheel and Axle
3. Pulley
4. Inclined Plane
5. Wedge
6. Screw

presentation_slides.title: Functional Classification
content: Force Multipliers: Load is greater than effort (e.g., lever).
Speed Multipliers: Load moves a greater distance than the effort (e.g., bicycle).
Direction Changers: Load moves in a different direction than the effort (e.g., fixed pulley).

sections.section_title: Mechanical Advantage, Velocity Ratio and Efficiency

presentation_slides.title: Mechanical Advantage (M.A)
content: The ratio of load to effort.
Formula: M.A = Load / Effort.
It compares the force you get out to the force you put in.
If M.A > 1, the machine is a force multiplier.
It has no units.

presentation_slides.title: Velocity Ratio (V.R)
content: The ratio of the distance moved by the effort to the distance moved by the load.
Formula: V.R = Distance moved by effort / Distance moved by load.
It has no units.
For a lever, V.R = d_E / d_L (distance from effort to fulcrum / distance from load to fulcrum).
For an inclined plane, V.R = length of slope / height.
For a wheel and axle, V.R = radius of wheel / radius of axle.
For a pulley, V.R = number of rope sections.

presentation_slides.title: Efficiency (η)
content: The ratio of work output to work input.
Formula: η = Work output / Work input.
It can also be expressed as η = M.A / V.R.
Efficiency is usually expressed as a percentage.
In real machines, efficiency is always less than 100% due to energy losses (e.g., friction).

presentation_slides.title: Levers
content: A lever is a rigid bar that is free to turn about a point called the fulcrum.
Three classes of levers based on the relative position of fulcrum, load, and effort:
1st Class: Fulcrum between load and effort (e.g., seesaw).
2nd Class: Load between fulcrum and effort (e.g., wheelbarrow).
3rd Class: Effort between fulcrum and load (e.g., fishing rod).

presentation_slides.title: Inclined Plane, Wedge, and Screw
content: Inclined Plane: A sloping surface; M.A = Load/Effort, V.R = Length/Height.
Wedge: Two inclined planes back-to-back; used for splitting. V.R = Penetration length / Thickness.
Screw: An inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder. M.A = πd / Pitch (d = diameter, pitch = distance between threads).

presentation_slides.title: Wheel and Axle and Pulley
content: Wheel and Axle: A wheel secured to a smaller axle. M.A = Load/Effort, V.R = Radius of wheel / Radius of axle.
Fixed Pulley: Changes direction of force; V.R = 1.
Movable Pulley: Multiplies force; V.R = 2.
Compound Pulley: Combination of fixed and movable pulleys; V.R = number of rope sections.

presentation_slides.title: Designing Simple Machines
content: Identify activities in the community that need simple machines.
Prioritize and select one activity.
Collect necessary materials.
Design a machine that includes at least two simple machines.
Build a prototype using locally available materials.

presentation_slides.title: Introduction to Waves and Oscillation
content: Oscillation (Periodic Motion): A to-and-fro movement that repeats itself over a fixed time interval.
Wave: A disturbance that moves from its source, accompanied by a transfer of energy.
Examples: Sound waves, water waves, waves on a string.

presentation_slides.title: Characteristics of Waves
content: Crest: The highest point above the rest position.
Trough: The lowest point below the rest position.
Amplitude (A): Maximum displacement from equilibrium.
Wavelength (λ): Distance between identical points on adjacent waves.
Period (T): Time for one complete cycle.
Frequency (f): Number of complete waves passing a point per unit time. f = 1/T.
Wave Speed (v): Distance the wave travels per second. v = f × λ.

presentation_slides.title: Simple Pendulum
content: A simple pendulum consists of a point mass (bob) suspended by a massless, un-stretchable string.
The period of a pendulum is given by: T = 2π √(L/g).
The period depends only on the length (L) and the acceleration due to gravity (g).
It does NOT depend on the mass of the bob.

presentation_slides.title: Spring-Mass System
content: A mass attached to a spring undergoes periodic motion.
Hooke's Law: The restoring force of a spring is proportional to its displacement. F_res = -kx, where k is the spring constant.
The period of a spring-mass system is: T = 2π √(m/k).
The period depends on the mass (m) and the spring constant (k).

sections.section_title: Propagation of Waves and Energy Transmission

presentation_slides.title: Mechanical vs Electromagnetic Waves
content: Mechanical Waves: Require a material medium to travel through (e.g., sound waves, water waves).
Electromagnetic Waves: Do not require a medium; can travel through a vacuum (e.g., light, radio waves, X-rays).

presentation_slides.title: Transverse vs Longitudinal Waves
content: Transverse Waves: The direction of propagation is perpendicular to the direction of vibration of particles (e.g., light, waves on a string).
Longitudinal Waves: The direction of propagation is parallel to the direction of vibration of particles (e.g., sound waves, pressure waves).
Longitudinal waves consist of compressions (particles pushed together) and rarefactions (particles spread apart).

presentation_slides.title: Production and Nature of Sound
content: Sound is a longitudinal wave.
It is produced by vibrating objects.
Sound requires a medium to travel through (solid, liquid, or gas).
It travels fastest in solids and slowest in gases.

presentation_slides.title: Speed of Sound
content: The speed of sound depends on the medium's density and compressibility.
Speed of sound in air at 0°C: 331 m/s.
Speed increases with temperature: v = 331 m/s × √(1 + T_c/273).
Speed in liquids and solids is higher and less affected by temperature.

presentation_slides.title: Reflection, Refraction, Diffraction, and Interference
content: Reflection (Echo): Sound bouncing back from hard surfaces.
Refraction: Bending of sound due to changes in its speed.
Diffraction: Spreading of sound around obstacles or through openings.
Interference: The combination of two or more sound waves.

presentation_slides.title: Superposition Principle and Interference
content: Superposition Principle: When two or more waves pass the same point, the resultant displacement is the sum of the individual displacements.
Constructive Interference: Waves are in phase; the resultant wave has a larger amplitude.
Destructive Interference: Waves are out of phase; the resultant wave has a smaller or zero amplitude.
Standing Waves: Formed by the superposition of two identical waves traveling in opposite directions.
Nodes: Points of zero displacement.
Antinodes: Points of maximum displacement.

presentation_slides.title: Pitch, Loudness, and Timbre
content: Pitch: Determined by the frequency of the sound wave. Higher frequency = higher pitch.
Loudness: Determined by the amplitude of the sound wave. Higher amplitude = louder sound. Measured in decibels (dB).
Timbre (Quality): Distinguishes sounds of the same pitch and loudness from different sources.
Sound Pollution: Elevated sound levels that can cause health issues like hearing loss and hypertension.

presentation_slides.title: What is Temperature?
content: Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body.
It is related to the average kinetic energy of the particles in a sample of matter.
Human perception of temperature is relative and unreliable.
Human beings are comfortable at room temperature (18°C to 22°C).
Temperature affects clothing, eating habits, health, and economy.

presentation_slides.title: Temperature Zones on Earth
content: Tropical Zone: Receives the most direct sunlight; high temperatures.
Temperate Zone: Moderate temperatures.
Polar Zone: Receives less sunlight; low temperatures.
Examples: Tropical rain forests (21°C to 31°C), Temperate climates (-3°C to 18°C), Polar winters (-50°C).

presentation_slides.title: Human Body Temperature and Safety
content: Normal human body temperature: 98.6°F (37°C).
To maintain this, the surrounding environment needs to be about 82°F (28°C).
Safety precautions for extreme heat:
- Stay well-hydrated.
- Wear appropriate clothing.
- Use sunscreen.
- Avoid extremely hot places.

presentation_slides.title: Global Warming and the Greenhouse Effect
content: Global warming is the increase in Earth's average temperature.
The natural warming of the Earth due to greenhouse gases is called the greenhouse effect.
Greenhouse gases include: Carbon dioxide (CO2), Methane (CH4), Nitrous oxide (N2O), and fluorinated gases.
Human activities (burning fossil fuels) are increasing the greenhouse effect, leading to global warming.

presentation_slides.title: Effects of Higher Temperatures
content: More frequent and longer heat waves.
Affects: Agriculture, Water supply, Energy, Health, Forests, Plants, animals, and ecosystems.
If current emission rates continue, temperature could rise by 4 to 12°F.
Big changes in energy use could limit the rise to 2 to 5°F.

sections.section_title: Measuring Temperature with Different Thermometric Scales

presentation_slides.title: Thermometer and Fixed Points
content: Thermometer: A device used to measure temperature.
It works by utilizing the expansion/contraction of a substance.
Lower Fixed Point: Melting point of ice.
Upper Fixed Point: Boiling point of water at sea level.
The space between these points is divided into equal parts to create a scale.

presentation_slides.title: The Three Temperature Scales
content: Celsius Scale (°C): Ice point = 0°C, Steam point = 100°C.
Fahrenheit Scale (°F): Ice point = 32°F, Steam point = 212°F.
Kelvin Scale (K): Ice point = 273.15 K, Steam point = 373.15 K.
The SI unit of temperature is Kelvin.
Absolute Zero (0 K): The lowest possible temperature (-273.15°C).

sections.section_title: Types of Thermometers and Their Use

presentation_slides.title: Types of Thermometers
content: Mercury Thermometer: Uses expansion of mercury. Range: -30°C to 300°C.
Alcohol Thermometer: Uses expansion of alcohol. Non-toxic. Range: -115°C to 78.15°C.
Resistance Thermometer: Uses the change in electrical resistance with temperature. Range: -270°C to +700°C.
Thermocouple: Uses voltage generated by two junctions. Range: -270°C to 2300°C.
Thermistor: Uses a semiconductor whose resistance changes with temperature.
Radiation Thermometer: Measures infrared radiation emitted by an object.

presentation_slides.title: Conversion Formulas
content: Celsius to Fahrenheit: T_C = 5/9 (T_F - 32)
Fahrenheit to Celsius: T_F = 9/5 T_C + 32
Celsius to Kelvin: T_K = T_C + 273.15
Kelvin to Celsius: T_C = T_K - 273.15
These formulas are derived from the fixed points of each scale.

presentation_slides.title: Design Your Own Temperature Scale
content: You can create your own thermometer using a bottle, straw, and alcohol-water mixture.
Use a real thermometer for calibration.
You can define your own unit and scale.
This demonstrates the principles behind thermometry.

presentation_slides.title: Thermal Expansion
content: Most materials expand when heated and contract when cooled.
Linear Expansion: The increase in length of a solid.
Formula: ΔL = α × L₀ × ΔT
Where:
ΔL = Change in length
α = Coefficient of linear expansion (depends on material)
L₀ = Initial length
ΔT = Change in temperature

presentation_slides.title: Coefficient of Linear Expansion
content: Different materials have different coefficients of linear expansion.
Examples: Aluminum (2.6 × 10⁻⁵), Brass (1.9 × 10⁻⁵), Iron/Steel (1.2 × 10⁻⁵), Lead (2.9 × 10⁻⁵), Glass/Pyrex (3.3 × 10⁻⁶).
Gases expand more than liquids; liquids expand more than solids.
Understanding expansion is crucial in construction to allow for gaps (e.g., in bridges) to prevent bending.
